Broken Chord Mr Homm

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: a point on the circle cuts the path from A through C to B into two equal lengths.
How to play: Drag the corners A, B and C, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick Names or Hint to show the labels or the proof, and press Reset diagram to start again.
Look for the math

Drag the triangle as you like: the point M always hands the broken path A-C-B to itself. That is the Broken Chord Theorem, credited to Archimedes, and this picture draws the construction Mr Homm's applet used to show it.

The claim

On the circumcircle of triangle ABC, P is the midpoint of the arc through C, and PM is perpendicular to the longer of the sides AC and BC. M then splits the broken line A-C-B exactly in half. If AC is longer, the claim is AM = MC + BC; if BC is longer, it is BM = MC + AC. The applet and this page use that exact wording, with the longer side chosen by comparing the two lengths.

How P and M are found

The perpendicular bisector of the chord AB meets the circle in the midpoints of its two arcs. The one on the same side of AB as C is the midpoint of the arc A-C-B, so that is P. Dropping a perpendicular from P to the longer side puts M on that side. Equality of the two arcs also gives equal inscribed angles, which is what makes the next step work.

Anderson's proof in the Hint box

Extend PM to meet the circle again at Q, and let F be where BQ crosses AC extended. Because QM is both an altitude and an angle bisector of the angle at Q, triangle AQF is isosceles and AM = MF. Since A, Q, B and C lie on one cyclic quadrilateral, triangle BCF is isosceles too and BC = CF. Put them together: AM = MF = MC + CF = MC + BC. The logic test checks both equalities on every generated case where AC is longer.

What the checks found

Over fourteen hundred triangles — corners on the circle and corners anywhere in the board — the claim held to within a millionth, and a second transcription of the applet's bytecode gave the same P, M, Q and F to within a hundred-thousandth. The old page notes one edge case: if Q happens to be B, use the tangent at B in place of BQ. The applet draws no tangent, so in that one case the Hint's F labels simply do not appear; the theorem itself still holds.

Try dragging C close to P, then away again: watch M stay put on the long side while the two halves keep matching.
